a120ud0-jun22-03:
Explain the wider authority and significance of the Sutta Pitaka. [AO1 20] 
 Features of stronger responses:
• Gave the context of the Sutta Pitaka within the Pali Canon and showed knowledge and understanding of the Pali Canon.
• Provided an overall explanation of the material found in the Sutta Pitaka in terms of its suttas and teachings.
• Explained its authority and significance through reference to, for example, specific passages such as the Parable of the Raft, the Kalama Sutta and biographical passages concerning the Buddha.
• Successfully identified and noted the significance of, for example, the Jataka Tales and the Dhammapada.
Features of weaker responses:
• Demonstrated confusion as to which Pitaka was being referred to with some candidates writing entirely about the Vinaya Pitaka.
• Gave a general response which gave brief descriptive details of each of the three pitakas.
• Showed some knowledge of the Sutta Pitaka, but were mainly descriptive – particularly of the life of the Buddha – without any consideration of the wider authority and significance of the Sutta Pitaka.
(b) ‘The Pali Canon is of little importance in Buddhism.’ Evaluate this view.
[AO2 30]
Features of stronger responses:
• Showed a full understanding of the three pitakas and considered the importance of each part in Buddhism.
• Successfully recognised and reflected on the difference in the importance of the Pali Canon to the monastic and lay Sangha.
• Demonstrated an awareness of the different types of Buddhism and whether, for example, the Pali Canon in general might or might not be as important as the Lotus Sutra or the Heart Sutra within Mahayana Buddhism.
• Considered whether questions regarding the oral transmission of the material which formed the Pali Canon undermined its importance.
• Noted the age of and the patriarchal background of the Pali Canon and assessed how these factors affected its importance.
Features of weaker responses:
• Tended to repeat in a descriptive fashion much of part (a) and consider whether or not it was still important today e.g., accounts of the life of the Buddha.
• Explained briefly the three pitakas and whether each one was important or not in simplistic terms e.g., the Abhidhamma Pitaka being important for bhikkhus, but not for ordinary Buddhists.
• Approached the question with an understanding of Buddhism as being a single united belief system and thus missed, for example, the distinction between Theravada and Mahayana Buddhism and how the Pali Canon’s importance is different for each.
• Attempted in a limited fashion to suggest that other aspects of Buddhism were more important than the Pali Canon such as meditation.
a120ud0-jun22-04:
Examine the concept of anatta with reference to the Chariot Passage in the ‘Questions of King Milinda’.
[AO1 20]
Features of stronger responses:
• Provided context by demonstrating sound understanding of the concept of anatta as one of the three lakshanas.
• Explained in detail and with examples what is meant by the concept of anatta including, for example, the concept of impermanence and of sunyata.
• Showed a sound understanding of the Chariot Passage identified in the question.
• Gave a summary of the dialogue between Nagasena and King Milinda and were able to name the five skandhas.
• Clearly linked the discussion of the nature of the parts of the chariot with the concept of the parts of the no-self.
Features of weaker responses:
• Gave a limited explanation of the concept of anatta lacking in depth and/or breadth.
• Identified anatta as one of the three lakshanas, but then described all three.
• Had very limited knowledge of the Chariot Passage and were thus unable to link it to anatta.
(b) ‘The three lakshanas (three marks of existence) accurately represent reality.’
[AO2 30]
Features of stronger responses:
• Successfully identified each of the lakshanas – dukkha, anicca and anatta – and considered ways in which they did or did not represent reality.
• Considered whether such metaphysical concepts could represent reality given their a priori nature.
• Linked anicca to modern scientific understanding of continual flux at a sub-atomic level and thus argued that it is successful in representing reality.
• Commented on the different types of dukkha and how each of these accurately represented reality particularly in the modern world.
Features of weaker responses:
• Tended to list the three lakshanas and describe with examples what each meant before a concluding paragraph which attempted to answer the question.
• Appeared to rely on the approach that if something was not understood then it did not represent reality – for example, most people do not understand/believe in no-self and therefore it does not represent reality, but most people do understand/believe in suffering and therefore it does represent reality.
• Were vague as to what is meant by reality and tended to focus on whether the three lakshanas were helpful/unhelpful in daily life.
a120ud0-jun22-05:
Explain different views in Buddhism about whether women (i) can be nuns and (ii) can attain awakening.
[AO1 20]

• Considered the question carefully and kept their focus on different views in Buddhism.
• Identified differences between Theravada and Mahayana with regard to women being nuns and attaining awakening.

a120ud0-jun23-01:
Examine the accounts of the conception and birth of the historical Buddha.
[AO1 20]
Features of stronger responses:

• demonstrated an understanding of the differences between biography/hagiography/
• connected key events to aspects of Buddhism in general e.g. birth under tree/s linked to the Buddha’s enlightenment under the Bodhi Tree.

a120ud0-jun23-05:
Explain the use of mindfulness in health care, education and business.
[AO1 20]

Compare the views of Gandhi and Ambedkar towards the Dalits.
[A01 20] This was a popular question. 
 Features of stronger responses: 
  stronger responses addressed the question directly with sound knowledge and understanding;  there was some impressive use of scriptural and scholarly quotes e.g. by Gandhi and Ambedkar themselves to exemplify points made;  they explained in detail why Gandhi opposed the treatment of the Dalits and yet supported the Varna system;  the comparing and contrasting of views was balanced and well supported.
Features of weaker responses: 
  there were also some very general and superficial answers to this question;  it was surprising to see a number of candidates who confused the views of Ambedkar with Gandhi;  others for some reason stated that Gandhi opposed the Dalits and supported the way they were treated.
(b) ‘The varna system can be justified.’ 
 Evaluate this view.
[AO2 30] 
 This was generally a well answered question with most candidates able to present reasoned arguments. 
 Features of stronger responses: 
  stronger responses were well developed focusing entirely on the issue raised by the question, were well supported, challenged and evaluated;  there were some good references to sources of wisdom and beliefs and concepts within Hinduism to support arguments e.g. the centrality of belief in varnashramadharma;  the answers were balanced in their evaluation of the positive and negative aspects of the varna system considering the value to Hindu society as a whole with the oppression of the Dalits. 
 Features of weaker responses: 
  they lacked challenge and evaluation of the issue and contained a number of repetitions of the same point e.g. the oppression of the Dalits;  arguments and views presented were not supported by evidence and examples;  the answers were imbalanced and were weak on the positive side of the varna system.

 between Brahman and atman.

The focus of the question was knowledge and understanding of Shankara and Madvha’s views on the relationship between Brahman and atman. 
 Features of stronger responses: 
  stronger responses made clear the differences between the two; answers referred to Shankara’s Advaita Vedanta and Brahman as being identical with the atman and Madhva’s Dvaita Vedanta which states that they are distinct from one another;  the answers were detailed and clear in their understanding of the concepts and were able to use religious terms and language confidently;  there were also some excellent use of quotes and examples to support the answers given.
Features of weaker responses: 
  some completely confused the views of Shankara and Madhva;  there was a lack of clear understanding which resulted in a lack of evidence, examples and quotations;  the answers were imbalanced and tended to focus much more on Shankara than Madhva. Although an answer cannot be completely balanced if it asks for the views of Shankara and Madhva then the higher bands cannot be attained Madhva is only afforded a short paragraph at the end of the answer.

 Evaluate this view.
[AO2 30]

  they gave a definition of what is meant by an impersonal God and were able to relate their arguments to Advaita and Dvaita Vedanta;  they were able to discuss, compare and contrast and exemplify the concepts of Brahman nirguna and Brahman saguna;  they also referred to the importance of the ‘personal’ in Hinduism and exemplified these arguments with reference to bhakti and darshan;  the responses contained thoughtful argument and a clear conclusion.

This question was the most popular within Section B, with an attempt rate of 47.5%. The facility factor of 53.3 and mean of 10.7 for this question, suggest that it was a fairly accessible question.

The question itself is very specific in that it asks how the Trimurti helps Hindus to understand the nature of God.
Features of stronger responses:
• contained thorough knowledge and understanding of the concept of the Trimurti, of the features of each individual god and the importance of those features in the understanding of Brahman e.g. the Trimurti representing the three main aspects of Brahman as creator, preserver and destroyer.
• they were able to discuss the importance of the Trimurti in the context of Brahman Nirguna and Saguna and how manifestations help Hindus in the understanding of the impersonal absolute.
Features of weaker responses:
• either simply described the Trimurti or explained some of their features without linking them at all to the Hindu understanding of God.
• others described or explained the main features of Vaishnavism and Shaivism. They simply did not answer the question set.
(b) ‘Hindus worship more than one God.’ 
 Evaluate this view.
[AO2 30]
The facility factor of 56.7 and mean of 17.0 for this question, suggest that it was an accessible question.
Most candidates were able to present some valid arguments to this question. However, a number of candidates did not refer to the central argument that all the gods of Hinduism are in fact expressions of Brahman.
Features of stronger responses:
• gave a range of valid arguments to support a balanced answer considering whether Hinduism is in fact monotheistic, polytheistic or henotheistic.
• were able to refer to relevant beliefs and practices within modern Hinduism and refer to the traditions of Vaishnavism and Shaivism which can be regarded as monotheistic in themselves.
• were also able to contrast this view with the belief that Shiva and Vishnu are expressions of Brahman.
• there were also informed references to ISCKON and the role of Krishna.
Features of weaker responses:
• were very superficial in nature and lacked evidence and reasoning to support the arguments given.
• there was also a lack of understanding of the terms monotheistic and henotheistic.

Features of stronger responses:

Features of weaker responses:  showed very limited knowledge of the topic and did not address the question in any detail;  listed certain events in the history of the Sikh community in Britain without any real development or examination;  described Sikh practices in Britain today.
(b) ‘Practicing Sikhism in Britain is not difficult.’ Evaluate this view. [AO1 30] Most candidates were able to present some valid arguments to this question. Features of stronger responses:  strong responses gave a range of valid arguments to support a balanced answer;  were able to refer to problems such as the use of Punjabi and strong sense of identity which Sikhs have making assimilation into British society more difficult;  referred to the freedoms in law which Sikhs have e.g. wearing a turban in the workplace which mean that they are not discriminated against;  there was considerable use of specific evidence and examples to support the views given. Features of weaker responses:  they tended to give general views which were not supported by evidence or examples;  arguments tended to be listed without being developed;  some answers were completely imbalanced focusing entirely on the difficulties encountered.
a120uf0-jun18-04:
Explain how the festival of Vaisakhi helps Sikhs to focus on the virtues of Sikh life. [AO1 20] The responses to this question were generally disappointing. Features of stronger responses:  addressed the question directly with sound knowledge and understanding of the festival of Vaisakhi;  were able to explain what the virtues of Sikh life are such as protecting the truth, the importance of community and a duty to oppose oppression and then link the practices of the festival to these virtues;  there was effective and coherent use of specific examples and evidence from the festival. Features of weaker responses:  there were some very descriptive answers giving the background to the festival and describing some of the practices associated with it;  a number of answers made no link whatsoever between the practices of Vaisakhi and the virtues of Sikh life;  there were answers which focused entirely on how Vaisakhi expresses Sikh identity which was only relevant to some extent.
(b) ‘The gurdwara is a social rather than a religious institution.’ Evaluate this view. [AO2 30] The responses to this question were generally disappointing. Features of stronger responses:  were well developed focusing entirely on the issue raised by the question, were well supported, challenged and evaluated;  referred to the social aspects of the gurdwara and its importance to the Sikh community especially in places such as Britain;  were able to show the religious significance and importance of the gurdwara in terms of worship, sewa and langar;  evaluated how the social and religious of the gurdwara are often inter-related, and that social aspects can be an expression of religious aspects. Features of weaker responses:  lacked challenge and evaluation of the issue and contained a number of repetitions of the same point mainly listing how the gurdwara is used by the Sikh community;  tended to be no more than a list of points for and against without any real development of the arguments;  no consideration of the relationship between the religious and social aspects.

b120u20-jun17-01:
Outline Aquinas’ cosmological arguments for the existence of God.
[AO1 25] 
 The standard here was generally good. A few candidates conflated the cosmological and the teleological arguments and seemed unsure which of Aquinas’ Five Ways formed the cosmological argument. However, most candidates were able to successfully identify the first three ways though there were variations on the amount of detail included. In particular, there was a lack of example/illustration and the rejection of infinite regression was rarely mentioned. Most made reference to the idea of motion, but only a few detailed potentiality and actuality. The second way of cause and effect produced more detailed answers. In the third way, the idea of contingency was mostly used correctly though few referred to necessary being and its implications for the argument. 
 Features of stronger answers  Clearly explained the arguments and appropriate examples/illustrations for example with potentiality and actuality.  Good explanation of why Aquinas rejected infinite regression.  Clear understanding of the distinction between necessary and contingent. Features of weaker answers  Elements of reasoning or key steps in the argument were missed.  Undeveloped explanations for each stage.  Some misunderstood the idea of “beings” and assumed they only referred to people. Hence contingent beings often had reference to parents and children.
(b) ‘Aquinas’ cosmological arguments are not convincing.’ 
 Evaluate this view. [AO2 25]
Most candidates successfully identified the criticisms of the cosmological argument from Hume and explained how alternative scientific arguments may be considered rival theories and so weaken the argument. A number of candidates discussed evolution rather than the Big Bang. The fallacy of composition, though often referred to was rarely understood. There were lots of quotes about mothers and the universe having a mother, but many candidates did not seem to understand how it connected with the challenge to the cosmological argument. Finally, evaluation is about weighing up the relative strengths and weaknesses of those arguments such that it leads to a justified conclusion. Those candidates who did evaluate, produced some excellent answers.
Features of stronger answers  Accurately identified key challenges and criticisms.  Evaluated the criticisms rather than just explained them.  Used philosophical terminology to identify the strengths of the argument e.g. logical, a posteriori, inductive reasoning, etc.
Features of weaker answers  Simply repeated challenges without assessing them.  Many candidates still interpret ‘evaluate’ as meaning ‘list the arguments for and the arguments against’.  Confused the challenges or could not explain them properly.
b120u20-jun17-02:
Outline the teleological arguments of Aquinas and Tennant for the existence of God. [AO1 25]
This question was not as popular as question 1, but nearly all candidates were able to address the arguments of both Aquinas and Tennant. A significant number of candidates answered on Paley – either because they confused it with the name Aquinas or because that was the only argument they knew. When explaining Aquinas, few made reference to the archer and the arrow and those who did rarely understood what it illustrated. Tennant’s arguments were generally well done and explained in depth with the majority detailing both his anthropic and aesthetic arguments. However, the lower band responses failed to offer detailed examples and seemed unsure as to how beauty points towards an intelligent designer. Features of stronger answers  Accurately addressed the idea of non-intelligent matter directed to a purpose according to Aquinas through the archer analogy.  Distinguished between Tennant’s anthropic and aesthetic principles.  Clearly explained the arguments with examples.
Features of weaker answers  Confused Aquinas’ argument with the cosmological idea of causation.  Could not clarify the idea of ‘purpose’ in Aquinas.  Conflated Tennant’s two arguments.  Digressed into Paley’s watch analogy.  Confused Paley with Tennant or Aquinas. 
 2.
(b) ‘Scientific explanations for order in the universe are more persuasive than teleological arguments.’ 
 Evaluate this view. [AO2 25] 
 In general, candidates offered a balanced response to this argument though answers often lacked a clear weighing up of the persuasiveness of the various arguments. Many candidates made reference to both the Big Bang and also evolution. Although the Big Bang is more connected to the cosmological, there is a case for referring to it in the design in terms of resulting order but this was rarely explored. Again, candidates needed to make clear why these theories are more persuasive than teleological arguments. 
 Features of stronger answers  Evaluated and commented on the persuasiveness of scientific data/arguments instead of just listing them.  Were able to clearly see both strengths and weaknesses in arguments due to their inductive nature.  Gave clear justification for their argument and appreciated the complexity beyond a simple ‘science’ and ‘religion’ divide.  Referred to arguments such as ‘God of the Gaps’ and considered the empirical evidence for evolution as opposed to the speculative conclusions of design arguments. 
 Features of weaker answers  Simply listed facts about the Big Bang and evolution.  Opted to repeat Paley’s design argument with no real references to science.  Struggled to clearly identify different lines of argument beyond a ‘science’ and ‘religion’ divide.
b120u20-jun17-03:
Outline the challenges to the ontological argument with reference to Gaunilo and Kant. [AO1 25] 
 Although a popular question, a surprising number of candidates attempted it not knowing Kant’s arguments. Candidates often began with a short explanation of Anselm’s argument in order to illustrate Gaunilo’s response. Reference was often made to Gaunilo and the greatest island but the conclusion was usually stated rather than explained. Although most knew that Kant’s challenge was linked to existence not being a predicate, they were not always able to explain its relevance. As always with part (a) questions, it is the lack of explanation in the candidates answers that limit the band they are awarded. 
 Features of stronger answers  Coherent explanation of Kant’s criticism concerning ‘predicate’.  Understood the ‘perfect island’ challenge and concentrated on explaining how Gaunilo reasoned this rather than a response to it.  Made good use of reference to Descartes’ triangle analogy and Kant’s response. 
 Features of weaker answers  Not selective enough e.g. explained the ontological argument from Anselm and then briefly the challenge by Gaunilo and then the response.  Could not really explain the idea of ‘predicate’ in relation to the argument.  Guanilo’s island challenge was stated, but not explained. 
 3.
(b) ‘The challenges to the ontological argument are ineffective.’ Evaluate this view. [AO2 25] 
 This question was rather weakly answered. Candidates were able to explain the response given by Anselm to Gaunilo although reference was not always made to Anselm’s second form of the argument. Higher band candidates were able to describe why and how the criticisms are ineffective in weakening the ontological arguments. At the lower band response, candidates often restated Anselm and Descartes arguments as explanations as to why the criticisms were ineffective but did not actually explain how Anselm and Descartes were more convincing than the criticisms. Modern scholars were brought in with varying degrees of accuracy and understanding. 
 Features of stronger answers  Used references and sources beyond Anselm, Gaunilo and Kant to good effect.  Introduced different lines of reasoning from the wider debate amongst scholars.  Discussed the issue of a ‘leap’ from concept to reality. 
 Features of weaker answers  Restated Anselm and Descartes arguments as explanations as to why the criticisms were ineffective.  Did not actually explain how Anselm and Descartes were more convincing than the criticisms.  Repeated the challenges without commentary or analysis.
b120u20-jun17-04:
Explain how Irenaean type theodicies offer a solution to the problem of evil. [AO1 25]
A few candidates erroneously discussed Augustinian type rather than Irenaean type theodicies. Most answers to this question tended to be in the mid-range. Candidates included both Irenaeus and Hick, usually beginning with the creation of man-made in the image of God but not in the likeness. Higher band responses then successfully explained the purpose of evil concerning the development of humanity and addressed the role of free will, epistemic distance and universal salvation. It was a shame that few candidates referred explicitly to the problem of evil and fewer took time to address how the theodicy provides a solution to this in terms of the benevolence and omnipotence of God.
Features of stronger answers  Accurate and detailed presentation of key Irenaean elements such as ‘image’, ‘likeness’, ‘soul-making’, ‘epistemic distance’, etc.  Good awareness of how John Hick developed the theodicy.  Clear understanding of the purpose of ‘epistemic distance’ linking it to both free will and development.  Explained all the above with a focus on how they attempt to solve the problem of evil. 
 Features of weaker answers  Confused theodicies.  Spent too much time outlining the problem of evil.  Had the general idea of evil serving a purpose of ‘teaching’ and ‘development', but either could not clearly explain how through use of appropriate examples.  Omitted key elements such as ‘image’ and ‘likeness’ distinction, epistemic distance, etc.  Merely presented the free will defence. 
 4.
(b) ‘Irenaean type theodicies are not compatible with the 21st Century world view.’ 
 Evaluate this view. [AO2 25]
Candidates who, in error, referred to the Augustinian theodicy in (a) did somewhat better on this question and were able to make general comments about theodicies and 21st century world views. Many candidates within mid- high range band responses were able to accurately explain general strengths and weaknesses of the Irenaean theodicy, but some did not always elaborate sufficiently on their points. This was mainly due to their responses highlighting the generic strengths and weaknesses of the theodicy and not addressing what is meant by ‘21st Century World view’. Features of stronger answer  Used the traditional strengths and weaknesses and related them clearly to examples from the 21st century and/or its world view.  An awareness of how lines of argument could be defended e.g. eschatological justification, but also the implications of this.  Made good use of examples of types of suffering to support an argument.  Some candidates made use of more recent presentations of the problem of evil pointing out the ways that the theodicy did or did not address them.
Features of weaker answers  Struggled with the 21st century world view.  Just listed one or two key challenges.  Gave minimal exemplification for supporting an argument.
b120u20-jun17-05:
Examine the nature of religious experience with reference to visions and mysticism. [AO1 25]
Surprisingly, this was the least popular question. Again, most answers were in the mid-range level. Candidates gave a general description of religious experiences along with examples of visions and mystical experiences, but only a few candidates explained the types and styles of visionary experiences. Examples were often not given, though some could give examples such as the Vision at Mons and good use was made of Muhammad’s vision. Candidates felt more confident when discussing mystical experiences. They were more detailed and most candidates successfully identified William James’ four characteristics of mystical experience. However, few students gave more than a brief overview of the general nature of mystical experience or the role of mystical experience within different faiths, e.g. Sufism.
Features of stronger answer  Use of James’ analysis of mysticism.  Good examples to explain visions.  An awareness of the overlap between the two.
Features of weaker answers  Unaware of what mysticism was.  Simply narrated a religious experience such as a vision.  Explained prayer and conversion. 
 5.
(b) ‘Visions and mysticism are valid means of communicating religious teaching and belief.’ 
 Evaluate this view. [AO2 25]
Higher level responses offered a well-balanced view of the arguments both for and against the validity of religious experiences from the perspective of Franks-Davies, Freud and Persinger. Occasionally, reference was made to Swinburne’s principles of testimony and credulity. However, a number of responses, as before, did not really tackle the demands of the question set and, in particular, failed to address the issue of ‘communicating’. Only the best candidates considered the unknowable nature of God. Features of stronger answer  Generally focused on the question set and used the traditional debates about the usefulness or meaningfulness of religious experiences.  Good use of different scholars to support arguments
Features of weaker answers  Just focused on whether or not a religious experience is valid in itself.  Repeated criticisms and challenges to religious experience without understanding the significance of these for the issue of communication. EDUQAS GCE AS RELIGIOUS STUDIES 
 Summer 2017
b120u20-jun18-01:
Explain the different cosmological arguments for the existence of God presented by Aquinas and Craig. [AO1 25]
The majority of those who answered this question were able to identify that Aquinas had three ways to his cosmological argument. Most were identified in the correct order. 
 Features of stronger answers 
 Examples were given, particularly dominos (they need to note this is not Aquinas’ own example) and some, yet relatively few referred to such concepts as ‘actuality’ and ‘potentiality’. There were some excellent explanations of Craig’s position, with succinct summaries and references to why there must be a personal creator. 
 Features of weaker answers 
 Few candidates referred to the Universe. It seems this should be a given, but often many stop at ‘everything inside the Universe needs a cause', without getting to the most important point. Less well known was Craig’s cosmological argument which did at times make the answer imbalanced. 1.
(b) ‘The Kalam cosmological argument is convincing.’ 
 Evaluate this view. [AO2 25] 
 Features of stronger answers 
 Where candidates looked specifically at aspects of the Kalam argument then they did it very well indeed. Some referred to the inductive nature of the argument or to its rejection of actual infinity. There of course was scope to look at unconvincing aspects of the cosmological argument as a whole, of which Kalam is a part, but the question must be differentiated from ‘is the cosmological argument convincing?’ Those candidates that recognised this scored more highly. 
 Features of weaker answers 
 Without an understanding of the Kalam cosmological argument it was very difficult for some candidates to evaluate at all. Many included general challenges to the cosmological argument.
b120u20-jun18-02:
Outline the different teleological arguments for the existence of God presented by Aquinas, Paley and Tennant. [AO1 25] 
 This question was often done superbly well. 
 Features of stronger answers 
 Candidates wrote with accuracy about Aquinas’ 5th way using his archer and arrow analogy to good effect. Thankfully they related this analogy to God and the Universe. The same applies to Paley, with the watchmaker analogy (please note it was nowhere other than a heath; there were some wonderful places where a watch was supposedly found!) To really make the point that Paley wanted to make, reference was made to the stone also as a contrast to the watch. 
 Features of weaker answers 
 Often candidates wrote about both Tennant’s anthropic and aesthetic principles, but few acknowledged any reference to evolution in the anthropic principle nor did they suggest that aesthetics are not necessary for survival. Simply mentioning examples such as the eye or the watch without reference to their complexity which is likened to the Universe, is a weakness. 2.
(b) ‘Paley’s view of the teleological argument is convincing.’ 
 Evaluate this view. [AO2 25] 
 Features of stronger answers 
 Where candidates looked specifically at aspects of Paley’s argument then they did it well. Some referred to the efficacy or not of the analogy between the watch and the Universe. Hume’s criticisms abounded, which were pertinent to the rejection of the analogy. There was of course scope to look at unconvincing aspects of the teleological argument as a whole, of which Paley is a part, but the question must be differentiated from ‘is the teleological argument convincing?’ 
 Features of weaker answers 
 General evaluation of all teleological arguments was not particular enough. Repetition of AO1 material was quite common as candidates searched for material to write.
b120u20-jun18-03:
Examine the ontological argument with reference to Descartes and Malcolm. [AO1 25] 
 Features of stronger answers 
 Many candidates validly introduced the ontological argument as deductive and based on logic. They then proceeded to set out a summarised version of its deductive nature which is valid. Answers showed understanding by using Descartes’ analogies of the triangle and the mountain and the valley. There were some fabulous explanations of Malcolm’s version. 
 Features of weaker answers 
 A fairly large number unfortunately wasted a considerable amount of time examining Anselm’s ontological argument. Some referred to Descartes’ definition of God as a ‘supremely perfect being’ though there were very few references to God’s essence, nor was there much understanding of the basics of Descartes’ view. Malcolm was generally tagged on at the end with few candidates really getting to grips with a complete examination of God as an unlimited being and the choice between his existence being either impossible or necessary. 3.
(b) ‘Kant’s challenge to the ontological argument is not effective.’ Evaluate this view. [AO2 25] 
 Features of stronger answers 
 Kant’s challenge that existence is not a predicate was generally well understood. It was pleasing that an example such as the thalers was included, that is that thalers in existence add nothing to those that are not. We read the car example often (please note this was not Kant’s example, but I am sure as a notion he would agree with it.) Davis’ counter-challenge to this though is that existence is a predicate as it has the property of ‘purchasing- power’. Use could also be made of Kant’s challenge regarding the noumenal world. 
 Features of weaker answers 
 General challenges to the argument were made. Whilst the main challenge to the argument is that existence is not a predicate it ought to be directly linked to the specifics of Kant’s challenges.
b120u20-jun18-04:
Examine the problem of evil with reference to Mackie and Rowe.
[AO1 25] 
 Features of stronger answers 
 There were some excellent examinations of the inconsistent triad, referring back to Epicurus. Use could be made of Mackie’s views on ‘unqualified omnipotence’ though to include ‘the paradox of omnipotence’. It is always evidence of a good answer that candidates are able to say that Rowe could see that some suffering may have a purpose behind it. 
 Features of weaker answers 
 The majority of candidates who did this question could refer to the idea of the inconsistent triad and apply the correct statements to the points of the triangle. Some erroneously put ‘omniscience’ in there and omitted ‘evil exists’ though. In the main it rarely went further than that. Rowe’s example of animal suffering was included, but candidates need to put his argument in the wider context of ‘intense human and animal suffering’. Some included Paul in this part which was irrelevant.
(b) ‘Modern problem of evil arguments prove that God does not exist.’ 
 Evaluate this view. [AO2 25] 
 Features of stronger answers

The best responses had an implicit understanding of Mill’s development of Bentham’s Utilitarianism e.g. they could generally detail the ‘Higher and Lower Pleasures’, the ‘Harm Principle’ and the introduction of ‘Rule Utilitarianism’. Some candidates also successfully identified that Mill favoured what is now known as ‘Weak Rule Utilitarianism’. Some outstanding candidates weaved Bentham and Mill in together to illustrate the context of Mill’s development of Bentham’s Utilitarianism.
Weaker responses tended to either concentrate too much on Bentham’s Act Utilitarianism, leaving little time for Mill’s development, or in some more extreme cases just concentrate solely on Bentham’s Utilitarianism. Some candidates seemed well prepared to answer a question on Bentham’s Utilitarianism, but less so on Mill’s Utilitarianism. 
 1.
(b) ‘Act Utilitarianism is not relevant in modern society.’ 
 Evaluate this view. [AO2 25]
The best responses were able to clearly illustrate why Act Utilitarianism is or is not relevant in modern society, rather than just using generic arguments. For example, some candidates raised interesting points regarding the place of Act Utilitarianism in a modern multi-cultural democracy where British values such as tolerance should be upheld or using the non-religious aspect of Utilitarianism to justify the main reasons as to its suitability given the secular nature of some modern societies. In addition some candidates successfully compared the relevance of Act Utilitarianism, in modern society, with other ethics they had studied – including Rule Utilitarianism. 
 Weaker responses found it hard to fully link the strengths and weaknesses of Act Utilitarianism into the question set. Therefore, the candidate would write simple examinations of the strengths and weakness rather than a discussion on the unsuitability of Act Utilitarianism in society today. Therefore, weaker responses tended to just have lots of generic 'pros' and 'cons' of Act Utilitarianism without either developing the points made or linking them to the AO2 question set. The best responses were able to successfully explain Act Utilitarianism and then Rule Utilitarianism; therefore, implicitly illustrating the differences. Explain the four levels of law in Aquinas’ Natural Law. [AO1 25] 
 This was a fairly straightforward question that was answered well for the most part and was the most popular choice for candidates. 
 Features of stronger answers 
 The best answers demonstrated the relationship between the four levels of law and how each lower level was ultimately a reflection of Eternal Law. The strongest answers also exemplified their responses effectively where appropriate and were able to explain Aquinas’ understanding of the place of law in God’s created order along with the purpose of the law. Some candidates did muddle the definitions of the different laws or missed out eternal law altogether and some talked vaguely about moral law without understanding that their definition was of Aquinas’ Natural Moral Law. 
 Features of weaker answers 
 Weaker candidates did not write very much or gave an explanation of the whole of Natural Law, with its precepts, acts and virtues rather than answering the question. To some extent, a brief description of the precepts could be awarded for, where it was demonstrating Natural Law as the third level of the hierarchy. Where this was not the case, little could be awarded. Candidates could also make sure that they use the correct terminology for the laws, some talked about external law, teleological law or even brought in ideas from Situation Ethics or Utilitarianism. Others did not clearly understand the difference between Natural Law and Human Law or muddled the relationship within the hierarchy. 1.
(b) ‘Human law should be completely based on Natural Law.’ 
 Evaluate this view. [AO2 25] 
 Features of stronger answers 
 Some candidates who had misunderstood the part (a), managed to do well in this part (b). If they had understood the meaning of human and Natural Law, then they were able to exemplify well and link their ideas to modern ethical dilemmas such as abortion and euthanasia. Some candidates muddled the question and considered whether Natural Law should be completely based on human law or whether you can follow Natural Law if you are obeying human laws. 
 Features of weaker answers 
 Weaker candidates were not able to exemplify well on this question and whilst some were able to offer lines of argument not all evaluated them successfully. Many wasted time with a lengthy introductory paragraph explaining Natural Law or telling the examiner what they were going to evaluate and this reduced the actual amount of evaluation taking place. In addition, many lengthy conclusions did not conclude at all, but recapped what had been said in the main response, thus considerably limiting the ability to gain award.
b120u30-jun18-02:
Explain the virtues and the acts within Aquinas’ Natural Law. [AO1 25] 
 The biggest challenge that candidates faced here, was trying to avoid conflating Aquinas’ virtues with Virtue Theory from Aristotle. 
 Features of stronger answers 
 Stronger candidates were able to identify Aquinas’ four cardinal virtues and three revealed virtues as distinct from Aristotle’s Virtue Theory. The stronger candidates then went on to describe and exemplify the different between interior acts (our intentions) and exterior acts (the act itself.) Ideal answers went on to explain how both needed to be good in order for behaviour to be truly moral, and understood that a good exterior act with a poor interior act was still a good action, but would not lead a person towards the beatific vision. A few candidates effectively showed how this could be applied to double effect and this was credited. 
 Features of weaker answers 
 Weaker answers included descriptions of Aristotle’s or Jesus’ virtues or of Situation Ethics. Some simply wrote a long essay substituting the word virtue or act for precepts. Some candidates still struggled to remember which virtues applied to Aquinas and tended to dip back into a description of the golden mean or see fortitude and courage as separate virtues. Others wrote about real and apparent goods instead of acts. Weaker candidates also attempted exemplification of the acts, but struggled in that they allowed a person to be euthanised if the intention was good. Many missed out the acts altogether or did not know what this referred to and so gave a general run through of the primary and secondary precepts instead. 2.
(b) ‘The deontological nature of Natural Law means that it works in contemporary society.’ 
 Evaluate this view. [AO2 25] 
 Features of stronger answers 
 The strongest candidates answered this well, using key terms correctly and giving exemplification. They also were able to focus on the deontological nature of Natural Law rather than simply the strengths and weaknesses of Natural Law in general. Some candidates did not focus on this aspect of the question and some even argued regarding the teleological nature of Natural Law. Features of weaker answers 
 Weaker candidates did not always appreciate the extent to which contemporary society faces problems with Natural Law that Aquinas would not have foreseen. Those who used examples regarding murder, rape or war, did not demonstrate the contemporary problems. Those who noticed that the nature of war had changed, or that abortion and other medical procedures are now different and throw up new problems that a deontological theory cannot resolve, performed better. Others argued about deontological theories in general, without reference to Natural Law.
b120u30-jun18-03:
Explain why Fletcher rejects the ethical approaches of legalism, antinomianism and the role of the conscience. [AO1 25] 
 This was the least popular question. It could be interpreted in two ways; either candidates thought the question asked why Fletcher rejected conscience, or they thought that a description of the role of conscience was required. Either approach was credited if candidates answered correctly 
 Features of stronger answers 
 Many candidates did a good job of detailing the antinomian and legalistic parts of the question, but struggled with conscience despite it being on the specification. Very good answers pointed out that Legalism went against Fletchers principle of personalism and were able to say why. They also showed that antinomianism was not pragmatic as it did not work towards a loving outcome. Strong answers showed that Fletcher rejected a traditional understanding of conscience, such as you might find in the church, as the voice or God, or an intuitive standard of goodness to measure our actions with. They also recognised that Fletcher saw conscience as simply the process of doing ethics and weighing up what to do, thus this interpretation of conscience means it is essential for Situation Ethics as one must weigh up how to act in each situation. Features of weaker answers 
 Weaker candidates confused conscience with consciousness. Some weaker candidates spent a long time simply describing Situation Ethics. Some description could be awarded for where it helped to demonstrate why Fletcher rejected it. Some tried hard to deal with the conscience, but did not really understand what Fletcher felt the conscience was. 
 3.
(b) ‘Following Situation Ethics leads to immoral behaviour.’ 
 Evaluate this view. [AO2 25] 
 Features of stronger answers 
 The best responses applied the appropriate principles of Situation Ethics and how this related to whether this lead to moral or immoral behaviour. Generally, candidates were able to make good use of examples and spoke about the practical nature of agape or the fact that from Fletchers definition of what is moral or good, it is impossible that following agape can lead to anything other than moral behaviour. Other good responses counter argued by saying that great and loving intentions can lead to horrific acts that other theories would regard as immoral. Weaker students did not evaluate their ideas but simply gave an argument in support of the question and then an unrelated argument against the question. Others used Mill in response to this question, which was awarded if they focused on ways of weighing up the morality of experimentation in each case, rather than application of his harm principle or other rules.
b120u30-jun18-04:
Apply Act Utilitarianism to the ethical issue of animal
experimentation for medical research. [AO1 25] 
 Features of stronger answers 
 Better answers showed awareness of the contents of the hedonic calculus as they applied it rather than simply spending time describing it at the start. Those that recognised that this was a complex issue that was difficult to assess, and why, were awarded appropriately. Strong candidates recognised that both Bentham and Mill did consider the suffering of animals in their evaluation of moral issues and included this in their application. 
 Features of weaker answers 
 Weaker candidates failed to actually apply much or any of the hedonic calculus or any Utilitarian ideas to the problem of animal experimentation. Candidates could have considered each individual act of testing or could have recognised the impossibility of this venture and considered whether we assess each drug / treatment or each disease or something else. Many chose to give a rundown of Bentham’s Utilitarianism. Some candidates had a good try at applying the utility principle to animal testing and were awarded but did little else and showed no real understanding of the issues that a Utilitarian might weigh up. Some did not mention Utilitarianism at all and simply gave a description of animal experimentation. 4.
(b) Following Act Utilitarianism results in injustice.’ Evaluate this view. [AO2 25] 
 This tended to be answered better than the part (a) overall. 
 Features of stronger answers 
 A few gave some good arguments concerning human rights, although not all candidates appreciated that human rights were a kind of rule or inviolable principle that might need to be overridden if it suited the majority. Where candidates mentioned scholars like Mill, this was credited when they were using him to evaluate whether there was a more just method of applying Utilitarianism. Some recognised the fact that you can’t please all the people all the time so it is just to serve the majority. Others even referred to that fact different forms of Utilitarianism developed to deal with the perceived injustice of Act Utilitarianism, e.g. Singer's version championing the rights of animals as well as humans. 
 Features of weaker answers 
 Weaker candidates failed to identify what the term ‘injustice’ meant . Once candidates have considered that justice is fair treatment or results and thus injustice means that people are treated unfairly, they might make some better arguments. Weaker candidates often seemed unprepared to weigh up how fair it is that we prioritise the happiness of the majority over the minority or mistakenly said that the minority were not considered.
b120u30-jun18-05:
Explain the challenges to Divine Command Theory. 
 Evaluate this view. [AO2 25] 
 This question was quite popular, and candidates were mostly able to address the three main challenges listed in the specification. They were credited if they were able to give other challenges as well or instead 
 Features of stronger answers 
 Good answers were able to explain how one strand or ‘horn’ of the Euthyphro dilemma led to the arbitrariness problem and were able to explain both ‘horns’ or strands of the dilemma. Good responses also were able to accurately state why the dilemma was a problem for the qualities of the Theistic God and thus for a definition of what is good. The best answers generally included all three challenges from the specification and understood that this was a meta-ethical problem rather than a normative one. 
 Features of weaker answers 
 In some cases, too much time was spent in re-telling the story of Euthyphro from Plato rather than actually explaining the dilemma. Weaker candidates were only able to give one branch of the Euthyphro dilemma rather than both. Quite a few candidates mistakenly attributed the Euthyphro dilemma to Robert Adams instead of Plato. 5.
(b) Divine Command Theory is a better approach to ethics than Ethical Egoism.’ 
 Features of stronger answers 
 Candidates were able to argue either way in terms of which approach to ethics was better and had some good ideas. The best answers compared and contrasted the theories enabling evaluation to be clear and the best candidates were able to exemplify their points. For instance, some pointed out that whilst one challenge to Egoism is that it is damaging to society, in fact it might be better than Divine Command here. This is because it emphasises the usefulness to the individual of working on a project as a union of egoists and is unlikely to be judgemental or condemning as Divine Command would be when people chose to reject rules. 
 Features of weaker answers 
 Many weaker answers gave lengthy explanations of Egoism and Divine Command theory before they began the evaluation. It is vital that candidates practice evaluating in an answer rather than just stating strengths and weaknesses. The band descriptors ask for candidates to engage with the topics for high-level response and this means that if they are arguing that Divine Command Theory is better because it offers clear rules that are universally applied, they can counter by saying why this line of reasoning maybe strong and what they problems there are with it. Equally, if they were to argue that Egoism is self- centred and doesn’t consider the needs of others, they should be able to say why the needs of others should be considered and why, in fact, this might not be a problem after all.

b120u30-jun19-05:
Explain the main features of Act Utilitarianism.
[AO1 25]
This question had one of the lowest facility factors (41.9%) of all the part (a) questions, suggesting some candidates found this question challenging (see features of weaker responses). Some candidates struggled to select appropriate information to address the question, they simply wrote everything they knew about Utilitarianism.
Features of stronger responses:
• Defined and explained the term ‘Act’ within Act Utilitarianism
• Used Bentham to exemplify the features of Act rather than giving a general outline of Bentham’s theory
• Gave ethical examples rather than non-ethical generic ones to illustrate features
• The strongest answers were able to describe the utility principle as not only producing pleasure, but minimising pain as well.
Features of weaker responses:
• Just gave an overview of Bentham with no reference to what made his theory Act Utilitarianism.
• Included extensive information about Mill or Rule Utilitarianism without utilising it to demonstrate the features of Act in contrast
• Were unable to explain or demonstrate how the aspects of the hedonic calculus might yield different results in different situations.

 Evaluate this view.
[AO1 25]

 Features of stronger responses:
• Were able to give reasons and examples for why Act Utilitarianism is effective or not
• Could contrast Act with Rule Utilitarianism and weigh up which approach was more effective

Evaluate this view. [AO2 25]

Features of weaker responses:

Explain John Stuart Mills’ development of Utilitarianism. [AO1 25] 
 Whilst this was a less popular question, it did attract many confident responses.
Features of stronger responses:
• candidates were able to explain what the utility principle was with accuracy by using Bentham’s statement of it and referring to both pleasure and pain.
• candidates were able to use Bentham to demonstrate how Mill developed the theory to eradicate some of the problems with it.
• the best responses focused primarily on quality of pleasure, higher and lower pleasures, Rule Utilitarianism and the harm principle. 
 Features of weaker responses:
• spent a long-time describing Bentham’s Utilitarianism, this did not allow them time to explore Mill fully and sometimes there was no link to Mill at all.
• listed all the features of Bentham’s hedonic calculus and showing how it would be applied.
• gave lengthy explanations of Foot’s Trolley Problem without reference to Mill. Some candidates believed that Bentham introduced the Trolley Problem.
(b) ‘Utilitarianism does not work in contemporary society.’ Evaluate this view.
[AO2 25] 
 Features of stronger responses:
• provided good examples and explored how Utilitarianism could work to solve modern problems like animal testing, nuclear weapons and more.
• considered that the answer might depend upon whether we are talking about Act or Rule Utilitarianism.
• explored how contemporary society is different from the society that Bentham or Mill lived in and consider whether Utilitarianism can be used to solve those problems that are relevant today. Features of weaker responses:
• did not differentiate between Act and Rule or produced more generalised responses about Utilitarianism.
• there was no recognition of Bentham or Mill’s role in law making and the justice system that still has an impact on the legal system today.
• regularly claimed that Utilitarianism and its goal of happiness was outdated without convincing reasoning.

Outline Joesph Fletcher’s Situation Ethics. 
 [AO1 25] 
 This was a very popular question for candidates. 
 Features of stronger responses:
• understood that this is a consequentialist theory and that moral judgements depend on each situation.
• developed the four working principles and six fundamental principles and defined key terms accurately.
• provided worked examples, and some could give examples that Fletcher himself used.
• used scripture to support Fletcher’s choice of agape. 
 Features of weaker responses:
• were unable to list any of the principles and talked about the issue of love.
• got bogged down in defining different kinds of love at the expense of summarising Fletcher’s theory.
• spent a significant amount of time detailing the context in which Fletcher was writing, whilst this was not irrelevant, caution should be exercised in an ‘outline’ answer that this is not at the expense of summarising the theory.
(b) ‘Situation Ethics clearly promotes justice.’ Evaluate this view.
[AO2 25] 
 Features of stronger responses:
• included some kind of consideration about what justice might be – e.g., fairness, or application of a system of law etc.
• were able to note the principle that ‘justice is love distributed’ according to Fletcher
• considered whether Situation Ethics was a Christianised version of Utilitarianism and therefore tried to promote maximum love for the majority.
• were able to use worked examples to show that it was not practical to use only love to try and produce justice – using Fletcher’s example of Hiroshima and Nagasaki, or using examples of their own to show how subjective or impossible it is to apply love. 
 Features of weaker responses:
• did not know what justice means and so spent some time just detailing the strengths and weaknesses of the theory.
• were unsure what love or agape referred to – seeing it as emotional feeling rather than an act of charity or kindness to others.
• did not provide any kinds of examples to support their claims.
• made claims about the selfishness of Situation Ethics that were unsupported.

• refer to a range of challenges to Divine Command Theory (there are 3 listed in the specification) rather just the arbitrariness problem.

• avoided restricting themselves to the two issues raised in part (a).
• made use of Adams and Baggini to evaluate the success of the arbitrariness problem.
• attempted to compare and contrast other ethical theories in an evaluative style to see if their approach was better.

• focus on analysing and evaluating the theory, rather than just reproducing AO1 type material.

The stronger candidates also examined the idea of panentheism, and the idea that the world should be seen as God’s body as opposed to the language of God as ‘King’ that reinforced patriarchal oppression of women. Weaker answers talked in more general terms about McFague’s idea that the idea of God as female would be more inclusive.
Features of stronger answers  Could clearly outline the different aspects of McFague’s responses to God being male.  Used subject specific language well and in the vast majority of cases this was fully understood.  Managed to explain McFague’s feminist critique of male language about God.  Offered accurate explanations of McFague’s alternative metaphors for the persons of the Trinity.  Engaged with McFague’s panentheist ideas and ecofeminism.  Detailed knowledge of McFague’s views but also showed understanding in the way in which they were linked back to the question.

(b) ‘The concept of God as mother helps Christians to understand more about the nature of God.’ 
 Evaluate this view. [AO2 25]
Candidates were able to refer to the advantages and disadvantages of McFague's position with the better responses presenting a balanced debate. Biblical evidence often helped responses to justify the different points of view presented. 
 Features of stronger answer  Balanced responses with biblical references used to good effect.  Showed an understanding and analysis of the language used for God in the Bible.  Recognised that the Bible was a product of a patriarchal society, arguing that feminine imagery would aid an understanding of the nature of God.  Engaged in debate and recognised the significance of McFague’s panentheism and how it contrasted with traditional Christian beliefs about creation.

For the more able candidates this was the opportunity to engage with the whole scholarly debate about the Trinity.

Features of weaker answers  Confused about the persons of the Trinity as co-eternal, co-existent and co-equal and the idea that all persons are fully God but distinct.  The counter-argument was often rather basic and there was a tendency towards a simplistic and Modalistic understanding of the Trinity (itself considered heretical in orthodox Christian theology).  Tended to repeat the same argument for each of the three persons.  Lacked a variety of views.
b120ua0-jun17-03:
Explain the views of Rudolf Bultmann on Jesus’ resurrection.
[AO1 25]
Answered well on the whole with most candidates being able to explain Bultmann's demythology in relation to the New Testament and the reasoning behind it in relation to the resurrection narratives. Few were able to successfully explain Bultmann's subsequent understanding of the kerygma that followed or indeed the specific emphasis that the victory over death was seen in the crucifixion. This latter aspect is the underpinning element to his rejection of the historicity of the resurrection in explaining why it was not needed from a Christian perspective not just a rationalistic view. Features of stronger answers  A good understanding of Bultmann’s demythology.  Examined Bultmann’s understanding of the resurrection as being the rise in faith of the church.  How this brought into doubt the historicity of the resurrection.  Had an appreciation of the balance between rationalism and faith in Bultmann’s ideas.
Features of weaker answers  Lacked a full understanding of Bultmann’s view.  Refer to demythologizing the text but not why.  Wrote more about N.T. Wright than Bultmann.  Clear misconceptions about Bultmann’s view that he was out to discredit Christianity.  Emphasised only the rationalistic approach of Bultmann. 
 3.
(b) ‘Bultmann’s views about the historical reliability of the resurrection make Christianity meaningless.’ Evaluate this view. [AO2 25]
The problem with this question was that many candidates, due to their incomplete knowledge of Bultmann, missed the thrust of the question and saw this as a question solely about the historicity of the resurrection, rather than the broader issue of whether Bultmann's interpretation meant that Christianity was meaningless. There was a tendency for this to become an attack on Bultmann by Wright, rather than appreciating Bultmann was arguing from a position of trying to defend Christian faith and make it more credible for the modern age. A few candidates clearly did not know who Bultmann was and confused him with Moltmann and the suffering Christ.
Features of stronger answers  Were able to identify Bultmann’s underpinning purpose of defending the Christian faith in the modern age.  Used the claims of N.T. Wright carefully in opposition to Bultmann’s view on the resurrection.  Debated and discussed the issue of what made Christianity ‘meaningful’ – faith or fact.
Features of weaker answers  Simply debated the historicity of the resurrection event at a basic level.  Confused the teachings of Bultmann about the meaning of the death of Jesus.  Presented Bultmann as anti-Christianity.

Examine the importance for Christians of the principle of love of neighbour. [AO1 25]
This was another ‘hit and miss’ answer that ranged from a good overview of the teachings within Christianity about love of neighbour with good use of biblical evidence to a simple re-telling of the Good Samaritan parable. There were quite a few vague answers that failed to extend beyond explaining that as a Christian it is important to be kind and helpful. Answers that took a less biblical approach were valid but the best ones gave concrete examples of how love of neighbour was demonstrated within Christianity. Features of stronger answers  Able to explore the links of Jesus’ teaching with Old Testament theology.  Linked the principle of love of neighbour to biblical references well and gave many practical and modern examples in support.  Understood the clear distinction between the Ten Commandments and the teachings of Jesus but the common ideal.  Identified and explained the context of the Greatest Commandment but did so selectively and accurately without retelling the parable.
Features of weaker answers  Often showed some confusion about whether the command love of neighbour was included in the Ten Commandments.  Wrote out the parable of the Good Samaritan.  Simple, generic points about love of neighbour in how a Christian may behave displaying limited knowledge and understanding.  There were a large number of responses that mixed up Bible teachings, which led to a muddled response. 
 4.
(b) ‘Love of neighbour is the only moral principle a Christian needs for today.’ 
 Evaluate this view. [AO2 25]
This was a question that could invite some very different and open responses with examples that could be drawn from anywhere within Christianity and across the course of study. The best responses took advantage of this opportunity and there were some very mature responses at the top end. Focus, however, remained upon love of neighbor as the only moral principle and many answers interpreted this in its narrowest sense as one religious principle against others.
Features of stronger answers 
  Well responded to in support of it being the only moral principle.  Analysed issues such as whether other concepts (e.g. conscience, truth, forgiveness) were more important.  Debated whether love of neighbour was already encompassed or underpinned other religious teachings.  There were some in-depth discussions at the top end that made interesting comparisons with other sources of morality or alternative moral principles, for example, agape and Situation Ethics and Natural Law.
Features of weaker answers 
  Answers were general and tended to focus on the notion of the principle of love verses the other religious laws.  Little understanding of agape shown.  The alternative view tended to be generic about how all laws are important.
b120ua0-jun17-05:
Explain different Protestant approaches to understanding the Eucharist in Christianity. [AO1 25]
This was answered well with most candidates being able to refer to consubstantiation, memorialism and virtualism that are the three approaches named in the Specification. In particular there was an excellent use of subject specific language and terminology. In some unfortunate instances answers earned little merit because they had confused Catholic and Protestant understandings of the Eucharist, either in part, or in a few minor instances just focusing on Roman Catholicism.
Features of stronger answers 
  Gave accurate explanations of the three main protestant understandings of the Eucharist.  Some good discussions offered and most candidates demonstrated that they understood both the similarities and differences between various Protestant understandings of the Eucharist.  Detailed knowledge and understanding of the Eucharist service.  Aware of the specific reasons for each approach taken.
Features of weaker answers 
  Spent too much time outlining the Last Supper.  Spent too much time explaining the Roman Catholic approach before answering the question.  Confused Protestant and Catholic approaches.  Confused the three Protestant theories. 
 5.
(b) ‘There is no common ground between Christian understandings of the Eucharist.’ 
 Evaluate this view. [AO2 25]
Many answers generally analysed the differences between Catholic and Protestant views, but recognised that there was common ground in that all denominations emphasised the importance of the Eucharist and saw it as a remembrance of the Last Supper. Some of the best answers also examined differences within Catholicism itself.
Features of stronger answers 
  Had a balanced view of both similarities and differences between the two traditions.  Explored the differences within, as well as across, traditions.  Made use of specific detailed differences to support the variety within Christianity.  Argued that variety did not mean contradiction and that just because there were differences it did not cancel out all sense of commonality i.e. aware of the complex nature of the debate.  Aware of the biblical context, references and common use of scripture. Features of weaker answers 
  Not being able to explore the nuanced differences effectively.  Saw this a general division between Roman Catholic and Protestant Christianity rather than as a more complex issue of variety of religious thought and expression.  Heavily dependent on differences and vague on similarities.  Did not draw upon the common biblical evidence of the Last Supper or reference to other biblical references to the Eucharist in the early Church. [AO1 25] 
 This was the popular question by far. The questions asked for the arguments supporting infant and adult baptisms. On the whole this question was answered very well. Most candidates were able to clearly examine the different reasons for both infant and adult baptism. Reference was often made to key scholars in the debate, for example Augustine’s argument based in the idea of original sin, or Barth’s support for adult or believer’s baptism. Best answers also used direct quotations from the Bible and were able to explain how they support infant and adult baptism. Weaker candidates were able to identify the basic arguments of the need to cleanse original sin and that adult baptism is a choice. There were a few weaker candidates who simply focused on baptism as a generic rite rather than infant and adult baptism as two separate occasions. More biblical support may have added depth to the answer. There was, overall, surprisingly little on the Holy Spirit and John the Baptist.
Features of stronger answers 
  Could clearly outline the different arguments presented by theologians e.g. Augustine, Zwingli and Barth.  Used biblical quotes and references to passages that supported either side of the arguments.  Managed to explain the differences between the views of Zwingli and Augustine on the role and importance of infant baptism and made reference to Anabaptists and Barth in supporting adult baptism.
Features of weaker answers 
  Lacked detail and failed to explore the arguments in depth.  Inaccurate use of scholars, confusing and conflating different views.  Generic responses that drifted into personal evaluation. 1.
(b) ‘Baptism is nothing more than a symbolic act.’ 
 Evaluate this view. [AO2 25] 
 This question was attempted well with candidates presenting clear evidence and arguments for and against baptism being symbolic. The best answers made reference to key scholars and Bible passages to support their answer. Weaker candidates made reference to baptism being a family occasion or party with no religious meaning. Stronger candidates focused more on a discussion of the arguments rather than getting bogged down in detail of explaining them. There could have been more focus on ontological change and the spiritual meaning of baptism. 
 Features of stronger answer 
  Clear critical analysis of the significance of different views about a sacrament and an evaluation of the significance of baptism for both faith and as a religious experience.  Used subject specific language well and theological terms.  Effective appreciation of the strengths and weaknesses of the different understandings so as to draw a reasoned conclusion.
Features of weaker answers 
  A brief ‘shopping list’ of reasons for and against the statement with little or no analysis of the reasons presented as fact.  A weak conclusion that often did not reflect the reasoning or evidence that was presented.  Generic responses that drifted into descriptions of baptisms today.

 Features of weaker answers

 Evaluate this view. [AO2 25]

Some responses included modern examples of charitable work done by Christian communities, therefore supporting the view that Contemporary Christian churches should focus on action and supporting the poor and needy. 
 Features of stronger responses: 
 ● Critical evaluation of communal living or charitable deeds. ● Detailed analysis of concepts such as ‘breaking bread’. ● Varied, modern examples to support arguments given.
Features of weaker responses:

Augustine’s views on infant baptism were addressed well by many, with the stronger responses including specific features of his views such as ‘ingrafting’. The understanding of Zwingli varied, with some believing he argued against infant baptism and others giving a very brief account of his views. The strongest responses explained his views clearly, referencing his view of baptism being a sign and seal rather than a way of washing away sin. Some candidates did not include views of Augustine or Zwingli, and as such did not fully answer the question set. 
 Features of stronger responses:
• demonstrated excellent knowledge of Augustine and Zwingli.
• provided a clear understanding of the biblical links to infant baptism. 
 Features of weaker responses:
• made no reference to Zwingli.
• incorrectly stated that Zwingli argued for adult baptism.
(b) ‘Baptism is for adult believers not infants.’ Evaluate this view with reference to Christianity. [AO2 25] 
 Many candidates tackled this question well, with some presenting persuasive arguments for either infant or adult baptism. Some candidates argued vehemently that infant baptism is child abuse, citing Richard Dawkins’ views. Many included Karl Barth’s views for adult baptism, and most presented his views well, in order to support their own arguments. Features of stronger responses:

Features of weaker responses:

[AO1 25]

In all cases, candidates had at least some accurate knowledge of the birth narratives in Matthew and Luke. Weaker responses confused the two accounts or included misconceptions. A few candidates conflated the two, for example believing both the magi and shepherds visited Mary, Joseph and Jesus in both accounts. Some candidates simply retold the birth narratives, describing what happened in each. In this instance, if the differences were made clear, this was creditworthy, but it limited candidates from achieving the higher bands, due to their lack of thorough engagement with the question set. 
 Features of stronger responses:
• demonstrated excellent knowledge of each account, explaining key differences such as the mention of Herod.
• provided a clear explanation of why the differences may have come about, e.g. redaction criticism.
• biblical references made throughout. 
 Features of weaker responses:
• basic misconceptions e.g. ‘King Harold’.
• conflating the two accounts (i.e., writing what happened in Luke was from Matthew and vice versa).
(b) ‘Redaction criticism is essential for understanding the birth narratives. Evaluate this view.
[AO2 25] 
 Again, with this question, a full range of marks were awarded, with some excellent arguments either for or against the need for redaction criticism. Stronger responses included a clear understanding of redaction criticism and linked this to viewing the Bible as a history or a theology book, arguing their view on which it is. Some brought in Bultmann’s demythologisation as another way of understanding the birth narratives. Weaker responses showed limited knowledge of redaction criticism and some candidates misunderstood it entirely. Features of stronger responses:
• explored a range of ways of understanding the birth narratives, e.g. demythologisation.
• used sections of the birth narratives to prove or disprove the need for redaction criticism. 
 Features of weaker responses:
• total misunderstanding of what redaction criticism is.
• confused arguments based on a lack of understanding of the birth narratives.

 Features of stronger responses:
• used direct biblical references used accurately and appropriately and expanded upon.

 Features of weaker responses:
• made no/little application of their limited knowledge and understanding to “… churches today.”
(b) ‘The main role of the Church is to provide religious teaching.’ Evaluate this view.
[AO2 25] 
 On the whole, this was answered well by those that selected this question. Features of weaker responses:
